title: Michigan Beats Western Michigan 13-12 on Restored Second, But Clock Sync Explanation Leaves Questions Unanswered
dek: No. 16 Michigan defeated Western Michigan 13-12 on a 47-yard Hail Mary with one second restored to the clock after replay review on September 6, 2026. The NBC broadcast clock showed 0:00 when the ball was initially out of bounds, but the Big Ten's replay system determined one second remained and that a Western Michigan defender made contact while out of bounds.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: Officials restored one second to the clock on replay review despite the NBC broadcast clock showing 0:00 at the moment of the out-of-bounds ball, reigniting the game for a second Hail Mary attempt that Michigan won.
bottom_line: The Big Ten's strobe-sync explanation addresses the technical possibility of a clock-camera discrepancy but does not address how replay operators determined contact occurred at exactly one second. The gap between what the broadcast showed and what replay officials announced remains unexplained in the Big Ten's public statement, leaving the foundation of the call unclear.
body:
No. 16 Michigan defeated Western Michigan 13-12 on September 6, 2026, on a 47-yard Hail Mary from Bryce Underwood to JJ Buchanan with one second restored to the clock after replay review. The play capped Kyle Whittingham's head-coaching debut, but it rested on an officiating decision that contradicted what the NBC television broadcast showed in real time.
Western Michigan led 12-7 when Underwood's first Hail Mary attempt sailed out of the back of the end zone with the NBC broadcast clock displaying 0:00. NBC play-by-play announcer Noah Eagle declared the upset: "TIME EXPIRES! IT'S THE ATTACK FROM THE MAC! WESTERN MICHIGAN SENDS SHOCKWAVES ACROSS THE COLLEGE FOOTBALL WORLD AND PULLS OFF THE WEEK 1 STUNNER!" Western Michigan's sideline had begun emptying onto the field in celebration.
Officals reviewed the play and determined one second remained on the clock.
The Big Ten cited technical protocol in its statement, per CBS Sports: "Eighty-five minutes prior to the game, all broadcast cameras used for the replay system, including the camera on the game clock, are synced using a strobe system to ensure all cameras are aligned." The statement suggested the replay system's clock reading, not the broadcast clock, was authoritative.
NBC rules analyst Terry McAulay questioned this reasoning on air. Per CBS Sports, he said: "The ball isn't even close to touching a player when it goes to zero. Their system, their hawkeye system, apparently either had a different sync or whatever, and they came up with one second when it touched a player. I don't see that happen. Assuming our clock is correct, it is clearly not touching a player. The ball is clearly still in the air when the clock goes to zero on our screen. The Big Ten is going to have to tell a lot of us how did they get to one second on this play."
Western Michigan coach Lance Taylor expressed doubt postgame. Per CBS Sports, he said: "I know when I looked up at the clock, it was past zeroes before we touched it. I knew that they would review it. It's the last play of the game. And because we defended it so well, I wasn't worried or concerned about our guys going out and defending it a second time. Unfortunately, we did not defend it as well the second time." Western Michigan president Russ Kavalhuna asked for a formal review, saying: "We'll talk to our commissioner and we'll try to see if there's anything that we can ask for a review on. Frankly, I don't know if we can. I just want everyone to know that this football team deserves a second look, if that's possible."
Kyle Whittingham told reporters postgame that he glanced at the clock after the first Hail Mary sailed out and believed one second remained, per CBS Sports. "That, obviously, is not up to me. The refs went to replay, and they confirmed it and gave us one more opportunity."
On the second attempt, Michigan scored the winning touchdown. The final margin masked what had been a tightly contested game.
